title: The Data Protection Act, 2019: Is Your Business Compliant?
author: Aisha S. Mohamed
excerpt: Kenya's data-protection regime now carries real teeth. We outline the registration, consent and breach-notification duties every business handling personal data must observe.
body: Since the Data Protection Act, 2019 came into force, the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner has moved from guidance to enforcement. Fines of up to KES 5 million — or 1% of annual turnover — are now on the table for non-compliant businesses.

Any entity that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data is a data controller, and most must register with the ODPC. Registration is not a formality: it requires documented data-protection policies, retention schedules and appointed data-protection officers for qualifying organisations.

Consent must be freely given, specific and informed. Pre-ticked boxes and bundled consents no longer suffice. Businesses should audit every touchpoint — websites, HR systems, CRM platforms — and record the lawful basis for each category of processing.

Finally, breaches must be reported to the ODPC within 72 hours where there is a real risk of harm to data subjects. A tested incident-response plan is no longer optional; it is the difference between a manageable event and a regulatory crisis.

title: Buying Off-Plan Property in Kenya: Seven Legal Safeguards
author: Faith W. Kamau
excerpt: Off-plan purchases can deliver real value — or real heartbreak. These are the contractual and statutory protections your advocate must insist on before you pay a deposit.
body: Off-plan property offers attractive entry prices, but the buyer shoulders the risk of a building that does not yet exist. The first safeguard is verification: confirm the developer's title, the project's approvals from the county government and NCA registration of the contractor.

Second, your sale agreement must contain a completion date with liquidated damages for delay, a clear specification schedule, and an escrow or staged-payment structure tied to certified construction milestones — never calendar dates alone.
Third, insist on a performance bond or bank guarantee where the deposit is significant. Fourth, register a caveat against the parent title so the land cannot be sold or charged behind your back.

Fifth, check the sectional-properties status of the development; sixth, confirm who bears the cost of the management company before handover; and seventh, ensure dispute resolution is by arbitration in Nairobi, not in a jurisdiction convenient only to the developer.
A thorough advocate turns an off-plan gamble into a structured, enforceable transaction. The cost of due diligence is a fraction of the cost of a failed project.

title: Why Every Founder Needs a Shareholders' Agreement
author: Brian K. Otieno
excerpt: A handshake and the Companies Act defaults are not a governance strategy. Here is what a well-drafted shareholders' agreement actually protects.
body: Most founder disputes we litigate share one feature: no shareholders' agreement. The Companies Act, 2015 provides default rules, but defaults are written for the average company — not for yours.

A proper agreement addresses the five pressure points: decision-making thresholds and reserved matters; share-transfer restrictions including rights of first refusal, tag-along and drag-along rights; dividend policy; founder vesting and good-leaver/bad-leaver provisions; and deadlock-breaking mechanisms.

Without transfer restrictions, your co-founder can sell to a competitor. Without reserved matters, majority holders can dilute you, borrow against the company, or sell its core assets. Without deadlock provisions, a 50:50 venture can grind to paralysis.
The agreement costs a fraction of one day in court. It is the cheapest insurance a founding team will ever buy — and investors will demand it before wiring a shilling.

title: Succession Planning: The Conversation Kenyan Families Avoid
author: William Majanja
excerpt: Intestacy triggers the Law of Succession Act's rigid formulas and years of court supervision. A will, properly drawn, restores your voice.
body: When a Kenyan dies without a will, the Law of Succession Act decides who inherits — and the court supervises the process through grant of letters of administration, confirmation, and distribution. The average intestate estate takes years, not months.

A valid will requires writing, your signature, and two competent witnesses present at the same time. Beyond the will itself, consider trusts for minor children, life insurance nominations, and clear records of matrimonial property.
Equally important is what happens before death: enduring powers of attorney for incapacity, and candid family conversations that defuse the disputes we so often litigate after the funeral.
Succession planning is not morbid — it is the final act of care for the people you love. Our family and succession team handles these matters with the discretion they deserve.

title: Arbitration vs Litigation: Choosing the Right Forum
author: Daniel M. Kiprop
excerpt: Speed, confidentiality and enforceability pull towards arbitration; cost dynamics and appellate rights pull towards court. The right answer is contract-specific.
body: Kenya's Arbitration Act, 1995 and the NCIA Act give parties a mature framework for private dispute resolution. Arbitration offers confidentiality, party-chosen decision-makers, and awards enforceable across 170+ New York Convention states.

Litigation offers coercive powers arbitrators lack — interlocutory injunctions against third parties, joinder of non-signatories, and a structured appellate ladder. For debt recovery against recalcitrant local defendants, the courts' summary-judgment procedures are often faster and cheaper.
The decisive questions: Do you need confidentiality? Is the counterparty's solvency doubtful? Will you enforce abroad? Are multiple parties involved who did not sign the arbitration clause?
We draft dispute-resolution clauses as engineered instruments, not boilerplate — because the clause you sign today decides the forum you fight in tomorrow.

title: Fair Terminations Under the Employment Act: A Checklist for Employers
author: Daniel M. Kiprop
excerpt: Substantive justification plus procedural fairness — miss either limb and the termination is unfair, however genuine the reason.
body: Kenyan courts apply a two-limb test to every termination: a valid, fair reason (substantive fairness) and a fair process (procedural fairness). Section 45 of the Employment Act makes a termination unfair if either limb fails.

Procedurally, section 41 demands that the employee be notified of the charges in a language they understand, be given a genuine opportunity to respond, and be entitled to have a fellow employee or union representative present. A hearing is mandatory even where guilt seems obvious.
Substantively, the employer must prove the reason — poor performance requires documented warnings and a chance to improve; misconduct requires investigation proportionate to the allegation.

Remedies for unfair termination reach up to 12 months' gross wages plus reinstatement in limited cases. A disciplined pre-termination checklist — charges, hearing, reasoned decision, right of appeal — is the employer's best defence.
